planting.note: Direct sow in hills after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Triple Treat earns its name by combining a decorative round orange fruit, pie-quality flesh, and hull-less seeds that can be roasted without shelling.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, thinning to two or three vigorous plants per hill. Triple Treat produces a 6 to 8 pound jack-o-lantern-shaped pumpkin whose flesh is sweeter and less watery than typical carving pumpkins, but the real distinction is its naked, hull-less seeds, which can be scooped out, rinsed, and roasted directly without the tough seed coat found in most pumpkin varieties. Harvest once the rind has hardened fully and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week before moving to cool storage. Because it excels at carving, baking, and snacking all from one fruit, it rewards gardeners who want maximum use from a single vine.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Gill's Golden Pippin Acorn Squash (Heirloom Golden-Skinned Acorn Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed; Gill's Golden Pippin is a semi-bush heirloom acorn squash with golden-yellow rind rather than the dark green skin of standard acorn types.

directions: Sow seed directly in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing hills to give the semi-vining plants room without the sprawl of a full-size squash vine. This heirloom stands apart from the ubiquitous dark green acorn squash by ripening to a bright golden-orange rind, and its dry, fine-grained flesh has a milder, sweeter flavor that many gardeners prefer for baking and stuffing. Harvest once fruit reaches full color and the stem has begun to dry and cork over, since acorn types do not continue to ripen off the vine. It stores for two to three months in a cool, dry spot, making it a good keeper for a squash that matures relatively early in the season.

common_name: Gold Medallion Squash (Hybrid Buttercup-Type Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Gold Medallion is a commercial hybrid buttercup-type squash bred for uniform fruit size and reliable yields for market growers.

directions: Direct sow seed in hills spaced widely apart in rich, well-drained soil, since vines run vigorously across the season. Gold Medallion is a hybrid buttercup-type squash that sets a heavy crop of uniform, 3 to 4 pound, deep-orange fruit with the characteristic small button at the blossom end, and its dense, dry, sweet flesh cooks up well for baking and pureeing. Growers value it for setting fruit reliably even under variable weather, giving a more consistent harvest than many open-pollinated buttercup strains. Harvest when the rind has hardened and the vine begins to decline, then cure for one to two weeks in a warm space before moving to cool storage to concentrate the sugars.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Hooligan is an All-America Selections winner producing miniature two-tone orange-and-cream pumpkins on a compact, high-yielding vine.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, spacing hills so the compact vines have room to set their heavy load of fruit. Hooligan won an All-America Selections award for a striking two-tone pattern that splits each miniature pumpkin between deep orange and creamy white, a novelty look that has made it a favorite for fall tablescapes and porch displays rather than cooking. A single vine can produce dozens of the palm-sized fruits over the season, giving far more usable pieces per plant than standard-size decorative pumpkins. Harvest once the rind fully hardens and the color pattern has set, and the small size means the whole crop keeps well for weeks without curing.

common_name: Gargoyle Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Warty Bicolor Ornamental Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Gargoyle is an All-America Selections winner grown strictly for its heavily warted, bicolor orange-and-green ornamental fruit rather than eating quality.

directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun and well-drained soil, giving vines room to sprawl and set their oddly textured fruit. Gargoyle earned its All-America Selections award for an unmistakable look: dense, bumpy warts cover the entire orange-and-dark-green rind, giving each pumpkin a rugged, almost reptilian surface unlike smooth carving types. The tough, thick rind holds up well through a full season of fall display without softening, making it a durable choice for porch and entryway arrangements. Harvest before hard frost once color and warting have fully developed, and expect several fruits per vine across the season.

common_name: Solar Eclipse Pumpkin (AAS-Winning Black-and-Orange Miniature Pumpkin)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Solar Eclipse is an All-America Selections winner producing miniature pumpkins with a dark, near-black cap over an orange base, resembling a partially eclipsed sun.

directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun, spacing hills to allow the productive vines to spread. Solar Eclipse produces palm-sized pumpkins whose deep, near-black coloring on the upper half of the fruit fades into bright orange toward the base, a striking pattern that gave the variety its name and earned it an All-America Selections award for novelty color. Plants set a heavy number of the small fruits over a long harvest window, making it useful for gardeners assembling mixed miniature pumpkin displays rather than growing for eating. Pick once the color pattern has fully developed and the rind has hardened, and the small fruits need no curing before use in fall arrangements.

common_name: Hasta La Pasta Spaghetti Squash (Large-Fruited Heirloom Spaghetti Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Hasta La Pasta is an open-pollinated spaghetti squash bred for noticeably larger fruit than standard varieties, often 6 to 8 pounds each.

directions: Direct sow seed in hills spaced widely apart in rich, well-drained soil, since the vigorous vines need considerably more room than a compact bush spaghetti type. Hasta La Pasta produces oblong, pale cream fruit that dwarfs standard spaghetti squash, often reaching 6 to 8 pounds per fruit, so a single squash can provide strands enough for several meals. Once baked or boiled, the flesh separates into the same long, mild, pasta-like strands that make spaghetti squash a popular low-carbohydrate substitute, but the increased size makes it a better fit for larger households or preservation. Harvest when the rind has toughened to a deep cream color and resists a fingernail, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry location for two to three months.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Stripetti crosses spaghetti squash with delicata, producing cream-and-green striped fruit with sweeter, less watery flesh than standard spaghetti squash.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil, giving vines moderate room to spread. Stripetti combines the stringy, noodle-like flesh texture of spaghetti squash with the sweeter, richer flavor of delicata, and the cream skin striped in dark green makes it easy to identify at harvest or on a market table. The strands separate cleanly when the cooked flesh is scraped with a fork, but taste noticeably sweeter and less bland than standard spaghetti squash, appealing to cooks who want the low-carbohydrate pasta substitute without sacrificing flavor. Pick once stripes darken and the rind resists denting, and use within a couple of months since it does not store as long as full-season winter squash.

common_name: Amber Cup Squash (Small Red-Orange Buttercup-Type Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Amber Cup is a small, red-orange buttercup-type squash popular in Japanese and Korean cooking for its dense, sweet, dry flesh.

directions: Direct sow seed in hills after the soil has warmed, spacing plants to allow the moderately vigorous vines room to run. Amber Cup produces small, 2 to 4 pound, deep red-orange fruit with the flattened, ridged shape typical of buttercup-type squash, and the flesh is exceptionally dry, dense, and sweet, making it well suited to steaming, roasting, and inclusion in Japanese and Korean dishes where kabocha-type squash is traditional. Its compact fruit size makes it convenient for a single household meal without leftovers, unlike larger winter squash. Harvest when the rind has hardened fully and the vine begins to decline, and cure for a week or two in a warm spot before moving to cool storage.

common_name: Early Butternut PMR Squash (Powdery Mildew-Resistant Early Butternut)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Early Butternut PMR reaches harvest 15 to 20 days sooner than standard Waltham-type butternut and carries improved resistance to powdery mildew.

directions: Direct sow seed in hills after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills to give vines moderate room to spread. Early Butternut PMR was bred to bring the classic tan-skinned, orange-fleshed butternut squash to gardeners in shorter growing seasons, reaching harvest well before standard Waltham-type strains while carrying built-in resistance to powdery mildew, a common late-season problem on butternut vines. Fruit averages 2 to 3 pounds, a convenient size for single-meal use, with the same dense, sweet, nutty flesh gardeners expect from butternut squash. Harvest once the rind has turned uniformly tan and hardened, then cure for one to two weeks in a warm spot to improve storage life and sweetness.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Knucklehead is an All-America Selections winner covered edge to edge in dense, knobby warts over an otherwise standard orange jack-o-lantern shape.

directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil, giving the vigorous vines ample room since fruit can reach 15 pounds or more. Knucklehead won an All-America Selections award for a texture unlike any standard carving pumpkin: dense, rounded warts cover the entire orange rind from stem to blossom end, creating a rugged, knuckled surface that stands out in any fall display. Despite the unusual texture the rind stays firm and workable, making the fruit suitable for both painting and light carving around the bumps. Harvest before hard frost once the color has fully developed and the warting has set, and expect a long-lasting fall display since the thick, tough rind resists rot better than smooth-skinned pumpkins.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Goosebumps is a hybrid warty pumpkin producing dense, fine-textured bumps over a mid-size orange fruit, a finer texture than the larger warts on some competing varieties.

directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills widely to accommodate vigorous 15 to 20 pound fruit. Goosebumps produces an orange jack-o-lantern-shaped pumpkin covered in fine, dense bumps rather than the larger, sparser warts seen on some novelty pumpkins, giving it a distinctively pebbled texture that has made it popular with retail growers and fall-festival displays. The heavy warting develops progressively as the fruit matures, so color and texture continue to intensify right up to harvest. Pick before hard frost once the rind has hardened and the bumpy texture has fully developed, and expect the thick rind to hold up well through weeks of autumn display.

common_name: Polar Bear Pumpkin (Giant White Exhibition Pumpkin)
subcategory: giant white pumpkin for exhibition and carving

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into rich soil with generous spacing once soil is warm; Polar Bear is a giant-type squash bred for smooth, snow-white rind rather than the orange color of most large pumpkins.

directions: Start seed indoors ahead of the last frost, then transplant into deeply worked, richly amended soil with plenty of room, since fruit can reach 50 pounds or more under good growing conditions. Polar Bear stands out among giant pumpkins for its smooth, pure white rind, a striking contrast to the orange skin of most large exhibition types, making it a favorite for painted or decorated giant-pumpkin displays as well as competitive weigh-offs. Keep soil consistently moist during vine growth and fruit set, and remove all but one or two developing fruits per vine if maximum size is the goal. Harvest before hard frost once the rind has fully hardened and the vine has begun to decline, handling the heavy fruit carefully to avoid cracking the shell.

common_name: Mesa Queen Squash (AAS-Winning Compact-Vine Kabocha-Type Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Mesa Queen is an All-America Selections winner combining a more compact vine with deeply grooved, dark orange-red kabocha-type fruit.

directions: Direct sow seed in hills after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills to suit the shorter-running vines. Mesa Queen won an All-America Selections award for producing deeply ridged, dark orange-red kabocha-type squash on a plant noticeably more compact than typical maxima vines, making it a practical option for gardeners who want kabocha's dense, dry, sweet flesh without a sprawling vine. Fruit averages 3 to 4 pounds, a convenient size for roasting or steaming whole halves. Harvest once the deep grooves and rich color have fully developed and the rind resists a fingernail, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry spot.

common_name: Bayhorse Gold Squash (Short-Season Idaho Heirloom Buttercup-Type Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Bayhorse Gold was selected in a short, high-elevation Idaho growing season and reaches maturity earlier than most buttercup-type maxima squash.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing hills to give the vines moderate room to spread. Bayhorse Gold is a golden-orange buttercup-type squash selected by a home gardener at high elevation in Idaho, prized for setting a reliable crop of 3 to 5 pound fruit even where summers are cool and the frost-free window is short. The dense, dry, sweet flesh is well suited to baking and pureeing, matching the quality of better-known buttercup strains while maturing faster. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the vine begins to die back, then cure for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage.

common_name: Table Star Acorn Squash (AAS-Winning Semi-Bush Acorn Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Table Star is an All-America Selections winner producing full-size acorn squash on a semi-bush plant that yields earlier and more heavily than older open-pollinated acorn strains.

directions: Direct sow in hills after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants for the semi-bush habit rather than a full sprawling vine. Table Star won an All-America Selections award for combining a compact plant with an unusually high yield of dark green, deeply ribbed acorn squash, often setting more fruit per plant than older acorn varieties while reaching harvest earlier in the season. The sweet, fine-grained orange flesh is well suited to roasting halves or stuffing, and the smaller plant footprint makes it a good fit for raised beds. Harvest once the rind has darkened fully and the underside patch has turned from white to yellow-orange, then use within a couple of months since acorn types are not long-term keepers.
